---
title: "Structural patterns across languages"
---

> Match code *structure* — not text — so the same rule catches a real `panic()` call in Go, TypeScript, Rust, or Python without flagging the word in a string or comment.

A regex on `panic(` flags the call inside strings and comments too, and `StyleRule` matchers only understand Python's AST. The [`Pattern`](../reference/index.qmd) condition matches structure through [ast-grep](https://ast-grep.github.io), so `panic($$$)` catches a real call however its arguments are spelled, and never a string that happens to contain the word.

<!-- gd-embed: no_go_panic.py -->

## What it catches

```go
func h() {
	panic("boom")  // panic() aborts the process; return an error instead
}
```

## What it allows

```go
func h() error {
	return err  // returns an error for the caller to recover from
}
```

*The catch / allow split mirrors the hook inline `tests`, so it stays true as the hook evolves.*

## Run it yourself

```bash
uvx capt-hook --hooks docs/examples test
```
